title: Loops
subtitle: Every Member of the Party
martuIntro:
Four heroes. Four bars to draw. Write it four times? No. Write it once, and let Python walk down the line, yes?
You have seen loops already: `for member in party.members:` at the bottom of the spell book and the mana bars. Somebody else wrote them for you. Since then you have written recipes and lists of your own. Tonight you write them yourself, one pass at a time.
goals: Say why loops exist, and write `for item in items:` with an indented body
Loop over a list of sheets, read keys from each `member`, and call a recipe for each one
Keep a running total, with `total = 0` before the loop
Put an `if` inside a loop to pick out some items
Compare neighbors with `range(1, len(chalk_wall))`, and see the decay for yourself
Write a `while` loop that changes its value each pass, stop a loop that never ends, and leave early with `break`

exercises.title: Predict the loop
exercises.martu:
Four spell colors, one for each of you. To print them I could write four `print` lines. Or I write one, and let Python walk down the list.
A [[for loop]] runs its [[indent|indented]] lines once for each item. Each pass, `color` holds the next item:
```text
pass 1: color is "gold"
pass 2: color is "fire orange"
pass 3: color is "teal"
pass 4: color is "silver"
```
The `for` line ends with a [[colon]], like an `if` line.
One time round the loop is a *pass*. A `pass` line in a starter means something else: "nothing here yet". You replace it.

anotherWay.label: Down the line
anotherWay.text: Mar'tu walks down the line and taps each hero on the shoulder: gold, fire orange, teal, silver. Same tap, four times. The loop is the walk. `print(color)` is the tap.

anotherWay.label: A finger on a shelf
anotherWay.text:
```text
[gold] [fire orange] [teal] [silver]
  ^
  color
```
Your finger starts on the first jar, then moves one jar along each pass. When it runs out of jars, the loop is done.

anotherWay.label: The loop table
anotherWay.text:
```text
pass  color          prints
1     "gold"         gold
2     "fire orange"  fire orange
3     "teal"         teal
4     "silver"       silver
```
Add a fifth color, and the table gets a fifth row by itself.
`for color in spell_colors:` means: for each color in the list, do the indented lines.

checkpoints.text: Add a fifth color of your own to the list, in quotes. Mar'tu would pick `"violet"`. Then Run.
hints: Look at the list at the top. Each color sits on its own line, with a comma after it.

A new item goes inside the square brackets, with its comma:
```python

    "bread",
    "cheese",
    "plums",
]
```
The loop finds the new item by itself. The `for` line stays as it is.
Write `"violet",` (or a color of your own, in quotes) on a new line after `"silver",`, with four spaces in front.

48  48  47  46  44  41  37
^

anotherWay.label: Your name, their name
anotherWay.text: You can call your dog anything you like. That name is yours. Your school's name is not yours to change: other people use it. The loop variable is your dog. `chalk_wall` is the school.

2. It runs the indented line: `48 hours`.
3. Next gap, 48 again. Then 47. Seven gaps, seven lines.

exercises.title: Each member of the party
exercises.martu:
A roster is a list of sheets. A loop over it hands you one sheet at a time, yes?
`for member in roster:` means: take the first sheet and call it `member`. Run the indented lines. Then the next sheet.
Inside the loop, read the sheet through `member`: `member["name"]`, `member["mana"]`. Not `roster["name"]`. The roster is the whole list, and a list has no keys.

anotherWay.label: Trace table
anotherWay.text:
```text
pass  member["name"]  board
1     "Oogrish"     Oogrish: 18
2     "Gearshift"   Gearshift: 20
3     "Bomb Shell"  Bomb Shell: 24
4     "Lucky"       Lucky: 26
```
`member` is a different sheet on every pass, so the same line shows a different hero.

anotherWay.label: A stack of cards
anotherWay.text: The roster is a stack of four cards. Each pass, Python hands you the next card and calls it `member`. You read the card in your hand, never the whole stack.
At the bottom of the mana bars: `for member in party.members:` then `show_mana(member)`. `party.members` was the roster. `member` was each sheet in turn.

With other names:
```python

    print(label + str(jar["left"]))
```
A number needs `str()` before you glue it to text.
Write `line = member["name"] + ": " + str(member["mana"])` in place of `pass`, then `show_on_ley_board(line)` under it, with four spaces in front of each.

items.title: Looping Over a Dictionary
items.summary: Walk a whole dictionary: its keys, its values, or each key with its value, using `.items()`.
items.body:
A spell book is a [[dictionary]]: a name for each spell, and a cost beside it. You know how to read one key. Tonight, every key.
A plain `for` loop over a dictionary walks its [[key|keys]], in the order they were put in. The first example shows it.
Most of the time you want each key *and* its value. [[.items()|`.items()`]] hands them back in pairs. Each pair is a [[tuple]]: two values in round brackets, like `("rope", 2)`. You met tuples in the Tuples article. Write two names on the left, and Python puts one value in each. The second example shows that on its own.
So `for name, cost in spell_book.items():` gives `name` the key and `cost` its value, every pass. Two names, two things in each pair. Write only one name, and you get the whole pair, brackets and all.
[[.keys()|`.keys()`]] hands back only the keys, and [[.values()|`.values()`]] only the values. `sum(spell_book.values())` adds up every cost in the book.
You have seen this shape in the campaign: every hero's sheet was a dictionary, and Lucky's pack could be one too.

whyWrong.0: On the first pass `i` is 0, so `wall[i - 1]` is `wall[-1]`, the last gap: the first shrink comes out 37 - 48, which is -11.

choices: `Sip.` forever, until the site stops it
